title: Developers do not care.
body: ⭐ 1/5 Stars — Think Twice Before Investing Your Time in CPM2 EDIT: I reached out to the discord team and they specifically said “We do not restore or refund hacked accounts. This is company policy.” I would steer clear of this game. I’m writing this review because players deserve to know what can happen when they invest hundreds of hours into a game, only to have their progress compromised by a hacking incident and receive virtually no meaningful support afterward. I spent countless hours playing CPM2, building my collection, earning vehicles, and progressing through the game. Like many other players, I invested my time because I enjoyed the experience and believed that effort meant something. Unfortunately, my experience with the game’s support team has completely changed my opinion of the game. My account was affected by a hacking incident, and I lost 12 paid cars. Only 5 of those 12 cars were restored. Seven vehicles remain missing. After 2 weeks and all that time and effort, I was left trying to get a reasonable resolution from the very people responsible for supporting the game and its community. The response I received was essentially: “We don’t restore cars to hacked accounts. It’s company policy.” Let that sink in. A player gets hacked, loses vehicles they spent countless hours acquiring, asks for help, and is met with a policy instead of a solution. Apparently, the fact that an account was compromised is enough to leave a player suffering the consequences without a complete restoration or refund. What makes this situation so disgraceful isn’t just the lost vehicles. It’s the complete lack of accountability, care, and respect shown to the player. I understand that companies have policies. I understand that support teams have limitations and that not every request can be granted. However, hiding behind a blanket policy instead of investigating an incident and working toward a fair resolution is not acceptable customer support. If five of my 12 missing cars could be restored, why were the other seven left behind? What justified restoring some of my property in-game but not the rest? Where is the transparency? Where is the explanation? Where is the willingness to make things right? These are reasonable questions that deserve reasonable answers. Players invest their time, effort, and sometimes money into games because they expect their progress to mean something. When a security incident destroys that progress, the way a company responds matters. A responsible developer should take the situation seriously, investigate what happened, communicate clearly, and make a genuine effort to resolve the damage. Instead, my experience has left me feeling that once something goes wrong, the player is on their own. A WARNING TO OTHER CPM2 PLAYERS If you’re considering investing significant time into CPM2, understand what my experience has taught me, if your account is hacked and you lose your vehicles, you WILL NOT get everything back. In my case, 12 cars were lost, only five were restored by the Devs, and the remaining seven have not been returned. Support’s response was that restoring vehicles to hacked accounts is against company policy. I was not offered a complete restoration or a refund for the losses. I’m sharing this so other players can make an informed decision about how much time and effort they want to invest. THE BIGGER PROBLEM A game’s community is not just a source of players. It is the foundation of its reputation. Players recommend games to friends, create content, participate in communities, and keep games alive. That loyalty is earned through the experience developers provide and the way they treat their customers when things go wrong. When a player loses progress through a hacking incident and receives an incomplete restoration with no satisfactory resolution, that loyalty disappears. The hours I’ve invested cannot simply be handed back to me. Neither can the frustration of having to fight for a resolution that should have been handled with far more care. I shouldn’t have to beg for a fair outcome after an incident that compromised my account. CPM2’s handling of my situation has made me question whether the company genuinely values the time and effort its players put into the game. I wanted a resolution, not excuses. I wanted accountability, not a policy quoted at me. And I wanted the same consideration for all 12 missing vehicles, not a partial restoration that left seven unaccounted for. Until this situation is properly addressed, I cannot honestly recommend that players invest significant time into CPM2 without understanding the risk. My verdict: Disappointing support, incomplete restoration, and a serious failure to maintain player trust. Seven missing cars might be just another support ticket to the company, but to the player who spent countless hours earning them, they represent real time and effort that cannot simply be dismissed. If CPM2 wants to retain its players, it needs to do better than point to a policy and expect people to accept the loss. Players deserve transparency. Players deserve respect. And players deserve support that actually attempts to solve their problems. Based on my experience, CPM2 has failed to deliver those things when I needed them most.

title: CPM2 Needs Serious Optimization and Gameplay Improvements
body: CPM2 Needs Serious Optimization and Gameplay Improvements Car Parking Multiplayer 2 has the potential to be one of the best mobile driving games, but its current state is extremely disappointing. 1. Terrible performance and poor optimization I have both a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra and an iPhone 15 Pro Max, yet this game suffers from lag, low FPS, and excessive device heating on both phones. These are high-end devices, so why is the performance this bad? The developers seriously need to optimize the game, improve frame rates, and reduce overheating. Players should not have to deal with this on powerful devices. 2. Racing bugs ruin the experience Racing is supposed to be fun, but constant bugs make it frustrating. The game randomly takes away distance or time during races, and sometimes it becomes almost impossible to progress. How are we supposed to compete fairly when the game itself is working against us? Fix these bugs before adding more content. 3. Ridiculously expensive prices The in-game economy needs a serious rework. Cars and other items are far too expensive, and progression feels unnecessarily slow. This is not about wanting everything for free. Players should be rewarded fairly for the time and effort they invest in the game. 4. Progression is painfully slow I am currently level 3 and almost ready to reach Professional. I already own 17 cars, one house, and five businesses, yet leveling up still takes far too long. I have completed games like CarX Street and Racing Master, and those games managed to make progression challenging without making it feel like a second job. CPM2 needs a better progression system that rewards players and makes the game enjoyable instead of exhausting. 5. More cars and better support for mobile players The developers need to add more vehicles and pay more attention to the mobile version. It is frustrating to see so much attention being given to the PC version while mobile players continue dealing with performance issues, bugs, and an unbalanced economy. Mobile players are part of this community too, and we deserve proper optimization, regular fixes, and meaningful updates. Final thoughts CPM2 has great potential, but potential means nothing if the actual gameplay is frustrating. The developers need to prioritize optimization, bug fixes, fair prices, faster progression, and more vehicles. CarX Street and Racing Master show that mobile driving games can be challenging and entertaining without making players miserable. CPM2 needs to learn from its competitors, listen to its community, and fix the problems that already exist. Optimize the game. Fix the bugs. Balance the economy. Improve progression. Add more cars. Stop ignoring the mobile experience. Players want to enjoy this game, but the developers need to give us a reason to keep playing. If these issues continue to be ignored, community frustration will only grow. Less focus on unnecessary priorities and more focus on fixing the game. Listen to your players before it is too late.

title: Feature Request: Add Winter Spawn Location & Rename Race Track to Silverton
body: Description Since Car Parking Multiplayer 2 (CPM 2) already features a fully functional dynamic weather system and map areas like the Japan Suburban and Touge mountain zones, this request focuses on the remaining minor quality-of-life map updates. Specifically, the game is missing a dedicated Winter/Snow spawn point menu selection, and the current generic race track would benefit from being officially renamed to "Silverton" to establish its identity. Implementing these two changes will streamline navigation for the drifting community and finalize the professional racing theme of the track. Key Details & Implementation Suggestions 1. Add Winter Environment Spawn Point • The Issue: While CPM 2 features winter elements and seasonal snow regions, players currently have to drive across other zones manually to reach the snow areas. • The Solution: Add a dedicated Winter Spawn option to the main map teleport/spawn menu. This should drop the player directly into a snow-covered parking zone or a central location in the winter map region, allowing instant access to low-grip ice and snow drift sessions. 2. Rename Race Track to "Silverton" • The Issue: The main racing venue is referred to generally as the "Race Track" or confusingly associated with real-world titles like Silverstone. • The Solution: Formally rename the area in the UI, map markers, and teleports to Silverton Circuit (or Silverton Track). This aligns with the community identity and establishes a definitive, branded name for the game's premier racing hub. title: Revaluation
body: 1- Value adjustment and a money cap: raise the maximum limit to, say, 100 million, but without allowing just any ordinary car to be worth 50 million right off the bat, in order to prevent inflation. 2- A value scanner: the system analyzes the car—including upgrades, HP, torque, vinyls, and parts—and provides a recommended range (e.g., an estimated value of 20 million). If you set the price much higher than that, it warns you that there is a lower chance of the car actually selling. 3- A secure trading system: instead of relying on trust, implement a feature like a trade screen where both parties can see exactly what they are giving and receiving before confirming the deal. 4- Longer-distance races on a map that allows for top-speed driving (covering about a quarter-mile or more), plus a separate map dedicated solely to buying and selling cars, free from interruptions by other players who want to race. 5- Add more vinyls, rims, and accessories—especially for cars that currently lack them—and improve the vinyl editing tools, such as a feature that automatically applies the same vinyl to both sides of the car. It’s not a small thing, but it would improve the experience.
